overview: Bajaj Finance is India's largest diversified non-banking financial company (NBFC), part of the Bajaj Group, with a consolidated AUM of roughly Rs 5,84,624 crore (~26% YoY growth) as of September 2026 and a customer franchise of 128.85 million. It lends across consumer durables/digital products, personal loans, SME/MSME, commercial, rural, gold loans and microfinance, and consolidates Bajaj Housing Finance Limited (BHFL, ~87% owned, separately listed since 2024, AUM ~Rs 1,58,205 crore) and Bajaj Financial Securities Limited (broking/wealth, AUM ~Rs 12,058 crore). It is majority owned (~51.3%) by listed promoter Bajaj Finserv Limited and is regulated by the RBI as an upper-layer, deposit-taking NBFC-ICC.

business_model.summary: Bajaj Finance earns net interest income (spread between yield on a diversified, largely secured/semi-secured retail and wholesale loan book and its cost of borrowed funds) plus fee/non-interest income from cross-selling insurance, payments, wealth/broking and deposit products to a large and growing customer franchise. Housing/mortgage finance is written through subsidiary BHFL; broking and wealth management through Bajaj Financial Securities. Growth is funded by a diversified borrowing mix (money markets/NCDs, banks, retail/corporate deposits, ECBs) and periodic equity capital raises (QIP/preferential issues, most recently a ~Rs 17,500 crore raise announced October 2026) to maintain leverage within a self-imposed 5x-5.5x corridor.

revenue_streams.name: Consumer Finance (urban/durables, digital products, EMI Card, 2W/3W)
revenue_streams.note: % of standalone BFL AUM, urban book

revenue_streams.name: Mortgages (via BHFL: home loans, LAP, LRD, developer finance)
Rural lending (consumer durables, personal loans, gold loans, tractor, microfinance)
Commercial lending (mid-corporate, LAS, IPO financing, lease rental discounting)
Fee income / cross-sell (insurance distribution, payments, wealth/broking)
revenue_streams.note: non-interest income ~17% of consolidated net total income

business_model.customer_type: B2C (mass and affluent retail/consumer) and B2B (SME, mid-corporate, developers); deposit-taking from retail and corporate depositors
business_model.geographic_mix: India-only; present across ~4,091 lending locations (1,515 urban, 2,576 rural) plus 2,022 Gold Loan branches and 480 MFI branches as of Sept 2026; BHFL present in 182 locations

main_competitors: manufacturer/e-commerce captive financing (Samsung, Xiaomi, Amazon, Flipkart)
competitive_position.market_position: Largest diversified NBFC in India by AUM and customer franchise; a leading player in consumer durables/digital-product financing (management and third-party estimates put its share of organized offline electronics financing well above 50%), among the top 5 gold loan NBFCs, and (via BHFL) a large and fast-growing housing finance player that crossed Rs 1.5 lakh crore AUM in Q2 FY27.

moat_factors.factor: Scale of customer franchise and cross-sell
moat_factors.description: 128.85 MM total customer franchise, 82.36 MM in the cross-sell franchise (63.9% of total); product-per-customer metric is actively managed to raise wallet share across lending, deposits, payments and distributed products.

Backed by Bajaj Finserv (51.3% owner) and the broader Bajaj Group, one of India's oldest business houses; AAA domestic credit ratings (CRISIL, ICRA, CARE, India Ratings) support a comparatively low and improving cost of funds (7.31% in Q2 FY27, down 9bps QoQ).

Large proprietary data set across 128 MM+ customers; actively scaling an AI transformation program (FINAI) across sales, underwriting, fraud detection, collections and servicing, with hundreds of agentic AI deployments targeted for FY27.
Over 253,900 active distribution points (consumer durable/digital/lifestyle stores, dealers, DSAs) built over two decades, difficult for new entrants to replicate quickly.
One of relatively few large NBFCs permitted to take public deposits, aiding funding diversification (deposits ~14% of consolidated borrowings) alongside money markets, banks and ECBs.

weaknesses: Primarily unsecured/semi-secured consumer and SME exposure makes a meaningful share of the book more credit-cycle sensitive than bank-funded secured lending
As an NBFC (not a bank), it has a structurally higher cost of funds than large banks, compressing achievable NIM versus deposit-funded competitors
Reliance on repeated equity capital raises to sustain leverage within its 5x-5.5x corridor as AUM compounds at 23-26%, creating periodic dilution
Intensifying competition from banks re-entering consumer durable financing, fintech/BNPL players and manufacturer/e-commerce captive financing in its core durables niche
Upper-layer NBFC regulatory status brings bank-like compliance, governance and capital requirements without deposit-insurance-backed funding stability

growth_drivers: Continued AUM compounding guided at 23-25% medium-term corridor (raised to 26-27% guidance for FY27 after a strong Q2 FY27)
Bajaj Housing Finance scale-up: AUM grew 25% YoY to Rs 1,58,205 crore, now ~32% of consolidated lending AUM, with strong growth in LRD (+39% YoY) and home loans
New customer and cross-sell franchise expansion: 18-20 million new customers and 60-62 million new loans targeted for FY27; product-per-customer metric rising (6.11 as of H1 FY27)
Rapid scale-up of Gold Loan franchise (771 to 2,022 branches in under 3 years; targeting 2,700-2,800 branches by end FY27) and Microfinance franchise (480 branches across 11 states)

AI/digital transformation ('FINAI' / 'BFL 3.0') aimed at operating leverage: opex-to-NTI guided to improve 25-40 bps in FY27; AI-sourced disbursals already running into thousands of crores per quarter
Deposit book growth and cost-of-funds improvement, aided by AAA ratings and a diversified borrowing mix
Fresh ~Rs 17,500 crore capital raise (QIP up to Rs 11,700 crore + Rs 5,800 crore promoter warrants, announced October 2026) to fund continued high growth while preserving the leverage corridor

business.description: Stage 2&3 assets rose to 2.02% of loans in Q2 FY27 (from 1.87% in Q1), driven largely by a transitional increase in gold loan short-tenor schemes; unsecured consumer and MFI books remain more sensitive to Indian household leverage and income stress.

Banks re-entering consumer durable and personal loan financing, BNPL/fintech entrants, and manufacturer/e-commerce captive financing arms threaten share and pricing in BFL's historically dominant durables niche.

business.risk: Customer/product concentration in urban consumer and SME segments
business.description: A large share of profitability still derives from urban consumer durables, digital product loans and SME lending, which are discretionary-consumption sensitive.

financial.description: Leverage ratio of ~5.1x consolidated (standalone ~4.4x) sits within but near the top of management's self-imposed 5.0x-5.5x corridor, requiring periodic equity raises (most recently Rs 17,500 crore in Oct 2026) that dilute existing shareholders.

Cost of funds, though improving (7.31% Q2 FY27, down from 9.0% in Mar'17), remains structurally above bank deposit costs; competitive pricing pressure and rate-cycle shifts can compress margins (ROA guided at 4.3%-4.7% corridor).
Only ~14% of consolidated borrowings are deposits; the remainder is money markets, banks, NCDs and ECBs, exposing funding costs to credit-market conditions.

regulatory.risk: RBI enforcement actions on digital lending products
regulatory.description: RBI ordered BFL to stop sanctioning/disbursing loans under its 'eCOM' and 'Insta EMI Card' products in November 2023 for KFS (Key Fact Statement) non-compliance; restrictions were lifted in May 2024. Recurrence risk exists given the scale of BFL's digital lending operations and regulatory scrutiny of digital lending/KFS practices across the NBFC sector.

BFL has been classified by RBI as an NBFC-UL since FY2023 (and continues on the list through FY2025-26), subjecting it to enhanced capital, governance, disclosure and board-structure requirements akin to a bank, raising compliance costs and constraining some business flexibility.

regulatory.risk: Evolving digital lending / data protection / KFS rules
regulatory.description: Continued RBI tightening of digital lending guidelines, outsourcing norms and India's data protection framework could raise compliance costs or restrict product design across the large unsecured/EMI-card book.

macro.description: A meaningful share of AUM is tied to discretionary consumer spending (durables, personal loans, 2W/3W); a slowdown in Indian consumption or rural income growth would directly pressure disbursement volumes and credit costs.

RBI rate policy affects both BFL's marginal cost of funds and loan demand/affordability; rate cuts aid NIM and cost of funds but a hiking cycle would pressure margins given BFL's wholesale funding mix.
Broader Indian microfinance sector stress (over-leveraged borrowers, multiple lending) is an industry-wide risk that could affect BFL's smaller but growing MFI book.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Indian retail credit and NBFC AUM growth remains structurally strong, underpinned by rising financialization of household balance sheets, low mortgage/consumer-credit penetration relative to GDP, and continued digitization of lending; RBI's scale-based regulatory framework is pushing large NBFCs toward bank-like governance and capital standards over time.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate - consumer discretionary-linked lending (durables, personal loans, 2W/3W) is more cyclical; mortgages (BHFL) and gold loans are comparatively more resilient/secured
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - RBI policy rate moves affect both cost of funds (NBFC wholesale funding) and loan demand; management targets ROA 4.3%-4.7% and ROE 19%-21% through the cycle
key_input_costs: Cost of borrowed funds (money markets, bank loans, deposits, ECBs)
Employee costs (75,845 FTEs plus ~89,484 fixed-term-contract resources)

recent_developments.event: Q2 FY27 results: consolidated AUM grew 26% YoY to Rs 5,84,624 crore, PBT grew 29% to Rs 8,537 crore, PAT grew 29% to Rs 6,367 crore; added 4.42 MM new customers; annualised ROE 20.6% (up from 19.1% YoY); stock fell ~4-7% post-results despite strong numbers on margin/dilution concerns tied to the capital raise.

Board approved a ~Rs 17,500 crore capital raise: up to Rs 11,700 crore via QIP to institutional investors and up to Rs 5,800 crore via preferential warrants to promoter Bajaj Finserv (to help it maintain its 51.3% stake); first major equity raise since 2023, pending shareholder approval.

Gold Loan Stage 2&3 assets rose due to discontinuation of certain short-tenor schemes, pushing consolidated Stage 2&3 assets to 2.02% of loans (from 1.87% in Q1 FY27); management does not expect this to translate into higher credit costs and said underlying vintage credit performance (3/6/9-month-on-book) continues to improve.

At the 39th AGM, Rajiv Bajaj retired from the Bajaj Finance board by rotation and chose not to seek re-appointment (also exiting the Bajaj Finserv board), as he takes on additional responsibilities at Bajaj Auto including the KTM acquisition; Sanjiv Bajaj's director status was also changed from non-rotational to rotational.
Stock hit a record high with market capitalization briefly breaching Rs 7 lakh crore amid continued AUM growth and bullish brokerage commentary.

BHFL AUM crossed the Rs 1.4-1.5 lakh crore mark, growing ~24-25% YoY, cementing its position as the second-largest listed housing finance company by several measures; mortgages now ~32% of consolidated lending AUM.

RBI lifted its November 2023 restriction on sanctioning/disbursing loans via BFL's 'eCOM' and 'Insta EMI Card' products after remedial KFS (Key Fact Statement) compliance actions; restrictions had lasted about 6 months.

items.target: 23%-25% medium-term corridor (raised toward ~26%-27% for FY27 per post-Q2 commentary)
items.notes: Financial sustainability framework targets AUM growth in a 23%-25% corridor; management guided FY27 growth higher following a strong H1 FY27.
Part of the company's published 'financial sustainability metrics' framework alongside AUM growth, GNPA, NNPA, ROA and ROE corridors.
Consolidated annualised ROA was 4.6% in Q2 FY27 (vs 4.5% Q2 FY26), within the corridor.
Consolidated annualised ROE was 20.6% in Q2 FY27 (vs 19.1% Q2 FY26).
Consolidated GNPA/NNPA were 1.06%/0.42% as of Sep 2026, comfortably inside the corridor.
13.45 million booked in Q2 FY27 alone; YoY comparability affected by festival-season timing shift.
4.42 million added in Q2 FY27; total franchise 128.85 million as of Sep 2026.
Q2 FY27 opex/NTI was 33.0% vs 33.1% in Q2 FY26; improvement expected from AI/FINAI-driven operating leverage.

items.target: 150-175 new lending locations; 2,700-2,800 Gold Loan branches and 520-550 MFI branches by end FY27
items.notes: Geographic presence stood at 4,091 locations, 2,022 Gold Loan and 480 MFI branches as of Sep 2026.
Consolidated leverage was 5.1x as of Sep 2026 (standalone ~4.4x); drove the Oct 2026 Rs 17,500 crore capital raise.

guidance.management_commentary: Management characterized Q2 FY27 as an 'excellent quarter across all key metrics of AUM, new customer addition, credit cost, profit, ROA and ROE,' and said it remains 'optimistic about credit cost outlook for FY27' citing improving vintage credit performance. The Board tied the Rs 17,500 crore capital raise to 'strong India growth, underlying growth momentum of the Company and its subsidiaries and increasing focus on building resilience across various dimensions of business,' including capital position, technology/AI transformation, cyber resilience, regulatory compliance, provisioning coverage, diversified borrowings and liquidity.

bull_case: Largest and most diversified NBFC franchise in India, compounding AUM at 23-27% with a 128+ million customer base and rising cross-sell penetration (product-per-customer up to 6.11)
Best-in-class profitability for the sector: ROA 4.3-4.7% and ROE 19-21% targeted and consistently delivered, with AAA domestic credit ratings supporting a declining cost of funds
Bajaj Housing Finance is a second, fast-growing engine (25% AUM growth, ~32% of consolidated book) in a large, structurally under-penetrated Indian mortgage market with resilient asset quality

Heavy investment in AI/data ('FINAI'/'BFL 3.0') is already driving opex leverage, fraud reduction and underwriting improvements, a potential durable efficiency and risk-management edge over smaller peers

Strong capital position maintained proactively (leverage held within a 5-5.5x corridor via periodic raises, including the Oct 2026 Rs 17,500 crore raise), reducing balance-sheet risk relative to more aggressively levered NBFC peers
bear_case: Premium valuation historically assigned to Bajaj Finance leaves little room for error if growth or asset quality disappoints; stock fell post-Q2 FY27 results despite strong headline growth, reflecting sensitivity to margin/dilution concerns
Intensifying competition from banks, fintech/BNPL entrants and manufacturer/e-commerce captive financing threatens share and pricing power in its core consumer durables and personal loan niches
Recurring equity capital raises (2023 and again Oct 2026) to sustain growth within leverage limits create structural dilution for existing shareholders

Upper-layer NBFC regulatory status and history of RBI enforcement action (Nov 2023-May 2024 ban on eCOM/Insta EMI Card) highlight ongoing compliance and digital-lending regulatory risk inherent to its scale and product mix

Gold loan and MFI books are scaling rapidly from a small base; the Q2 FY27 uptick in Stage 2&3 assets (partly gold-loan driven) is a reminder that rapid branch/product expansion carries asset-quality execution risk
